title: What not to put on the site for an architecture studio
metaTitle: What to leave off an architecture studio site
excerpt: Cut the fullscreen render with no words. Keep built work, the constraint, and a way to start a project. A shorter site that tells the truth beats one that performs taste.
alt: Smooth overlapping waves of blue, violet, and warm orange, a polished surface with no building, no name, and no decision in the frame.
caption: Color with nowhere to stand. A practice site still needs a building and a sentence. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the first thing to remove?
faqs.answer: A fullscreen render or film with no project name and no constraint. It reassures the office and gives a careful client nothing to judge. Replace it with one built project and a sentence about what was hard. The rest of the cut list is easier after that.

faqs.question: Should we delete the journal and the awards?
faqs.answer: Move them below the work, or remove them if they are stale. A journal that has not been touched in a year, and an award ticker with no project attached, perform seriousness. They do not help someone decide to start a project conversation. Keep a true, recent credit on the relevant project page.

faqs.question: Is a shorter site worse for search?
faqs.answer: A shorter site with a clear purpose is easier to understand than a long one written to look complete. People-first pages answer the client's job: what you built, what you take, and how to talk. Pages that exist only to sound like an architecture office can go.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
The architecture studio website mistakes that waste a careful client's time are usually there to perform taste. A fullscreen render and no words reassures the team and confuses someone judging taste before competence. Keep built work, with the constraint named, and a clear way to start a project conversation.

A shorter site that tells the truth will outperform a long one that performs the idea of an architecture office. Cut first. Add only what helps the next client decide.

## The render with no words

Start here, because it sits on the first screen and it sets the wrong test. A cinematic image, often unbuilt, often unlabeled, fills the viewport. The office likes it. It looks like the images pinned above the desks. The client learns nothing they can hire: not the project, not the limit, not whether the building exists.

Replace it with one photograph of built work and one sentence. The sentence names the constraint. The button starts a project. Nielsen Norman Group's research on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is blunt about the first 10 seconds. That is the window in which a clear value proposition earns a longer look. A mute film spends the window on atmosphere.

If you love the render, label it and move it down, behind a built project. If you do not have built work yet, use the best real thing you have, even a small one, and label drawings as drawings. Do not open on a city you did not build.

Autoplay sound is the same mistake with speakers. Kill it. A client in a meeting will leave rather than hunt for a mute control. Motion that delays the sentence is the mistake in a softer form. The sentence is the point of the first screen.

## Pages that perform an office

Some pages exist so the site feels complete in a portfolio review. They are weak for a client with a site in their hands.

A manifesto that restates "light and material" without a building. A timeline of the founding with no effect on how you practice now. A map of every lecture city. A grid of software logos. A page called Explore. A stock skyline. An untitled mosaic.

[Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether the site has a primary purpose, and whether the content is for people who might come to you directly. The purpose is to help a client judge fit and start a conversation. Pages that would not help that person, if they arrived with an address, are candidates to unpublish.

A journal can stay when the essays help a client see how you think about a constraint they have. An essay that is a press release, or a year of silence with three posts at the top of the menu, should leave the header. You can keep the URL if something still ranks. You do not have to feature it.

Awards can stay on the project they belong to. A homepage ticker of medals, with no building attached, is the render problem in type. The client still needs the constraint.

## What a shorter site keeps

After the cut, the site can be small and still complete.

- A homepage with a few built projects, constraints named, and one action.
- Work, sorted so a client can find a building like theirs.
- The offers, in the client's words, each with an outcome and a boundary.
- People, with roles they will actually meet.
- The shape of the fee, if you are willing to say it.
- A contact path that says what happens next.

That set can be six templates. You do not need a custom layout for every essay. You need the photographs, the sentences, and a way to edit them on a Tuesday.

Hanabi's services are this kind of marketing site: structure first, then a build the office owns. If you are holding a long site and you want the cut made with you, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the pages you are proud of and the pages you suspect are theater. The studio designs and builds. It will not invent awards or a headcount you do not have.

Shorter is also easier to keep true. A twenty-page site drifts. A six-page site can be read by the principal twice a year. Truth is a maintenance problem as much as a writing problem.

## The work, the limit, the conversation

Whatever you remove, these three stay on the first screen and again at the end of a project page. The built thing. The constraint. The way to start a project conversation.

Check every remaining page against that trio. A people page that never links to their work has drifted. A fee page with no path to a conversation has drifted. A project page that ends on a credits block and a void has drifted. Add the missing piece back as a sentence and a link, not as a new campaign.

Use one label for the action everywhere. Start a project. Variations are how the cut gets undone, because each variation seems to need its own landing page. One label, one destination, one promise about the reply.

Keep the type readable and the images sized for a phone. A short site that is slow, or that hides the sentence under a desktop crop, still performs taste. The cut is not only pages. It is also the hero that says nothing.

## Mistakes that look like care

A few additions feel responsible and still belong on the cut list. A headcount you do not have, implied by a crowd of stock portraits. A founding year used as proof of judgment. A downloadable drawing set with no explanation of the move. A newsletter modal on the first visit. A second button that says "Collaborate" beside "Start a project."

Each one gives the office a sensation of completeness. The client gets another thing to interpret. Remove the implication of a larger team. Keep the real names. Remove the modal. Keep the building. Remove the duplicate button. Keep one label.

Unnamed projects are in this group. An archive of beautiful files titled "Residential 04" asks the client to do your editing. If privacy requires discretion, say "House, inner north" and the constraint, and skip the street number. Discretion is not the same as no words. A careful client can respect a private client. They cannot respect a folder.

Inconsistent facts are the costliest of these. The menu says alterations, the fee page says "select commissions," and the contact form says "tell us your vision." Pick the words from the emails you want more of, and delete the synonyms. A shorter vocabulary is easier to trust.

Check the site for claims you cannot point at. If a sentence says you stay through construction, the people page or a project caption should show who attends site. If nothing shows it, cut the sentence until you can. Performing thoroughness is still performing.

## A cut list for this week

Print the sitemap. Mark each item keep, move, or drop.

Drop the unlabeled render, the autoplay film, the stock skyline, the empty Explore page, and any form field that is not needed for the first reply.

Move awards under projects, the journal out of the primary menu if it is stale, and the long philosophy under a single paragraph on the people page or out entirely.

Keep the projects you can caption, the offers you want more of, the names of people who answer, and the contact promise you will honor.

Then load the homepage on a phone and read only the first screen. If it still requires the dropped film to make sense, you have not replaced it. Put the building back before you redesign the footer.

Do this before a visual refresh. A new typeface on the same mute render is the same site. Clients will feel the refresh and still not know what you built. The order is cut, then truth, then craft.

Share the list with the office before you delete. Someone will defend a page. Ask them which client decision it changes. If they cannot name the decision, the page can go. If they can, rewrite it until that decision is the heading. Do the rewrite in the same week as the cut, while the reason is still fresh and the old page is not quietly linked from the footer again.

## A different first screen, same standard

The standard travels. A guest deciding where to eat tonight is as impatient as a client judging a practice, and they are even more likely to be on a phone. The facts change. The refusal of empty atmosphere does not.

If the next site on your desk is a group of dining rooms, read [what the homepage has to prove for a restaurant group](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-a-restaurant-group). The first screen there is the room and one dish, plus a way to the menu or a table. A logo animation fails that guest the way an unlabeled render fails a building client. The cut is the same kind of courage.
